title: Review of JSS 2: Matter, Energy and the Five Kingdoms
summary: A quick revision of matter, its states and classes, energy and its conservation, and the five kingdoms of living things.

p: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (has volume). It exists in three states. A solid has a definite shape and volume. A liquid has no fixed shape but a definite volume. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume.

p: In JSS 2 you learnt filtration (to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid), evaporation (to get a dissolved solid back), sieving (to separate solids of different sizes) and decantation (to pour off a liquid from a settled solid).

Energy is the ability to do work. The forms you met are potential (stored), kinetic (movement), heat, light, sound, electrical and chemical energy. The principle of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed, but can change from one form to another. For example, in a torch the chemical energy in the battery becomes electrical energy, which the bulb changes into light and heat.

sections.h: A correction to a common idea
p: The lesson note calls fungi 'plant-like'. Fungi are not plants. They have no chlorophyll and so cannot make their own food, and their cell walls are made of a different material (chitin) from plant cell walls (cellulose). This is why fungi have their own kingdom.

title: Laboratory Conduct and Safety
summary: Ten safety rules for the laboratory, the safety equipment to know, and what to do when something goes wrong.

p: The laboratory is a place for discovery, but it can be dangerous. Chemicals can burn, glass can cut and flames can start fires. Safety is the most important rule in science.

1. Never enter the laboratory without a teacher or the lab attendant. 2. No eating, drinking or playing in the lab, because food and drink can pick up poisonous chemicals. 3. Wear protective clothing (lab coat, goggles) when told. 4. Read all the instructions before starting. 5. Never taste, smell or touch chemicals unless you are told to. 6. To smell a chemical, waft the vapour towards your nose with your hand; never sniff straight from the container. 7. Report all accidents, breakages and spills to the teacher at once. 8. When heating a test tube, point it away from yourself and others. 9. Clean your workspace and wash your hands before leaving. 10. Know where the safety equipment is: fire extinguisher, first-aid box and eye-wash station.

sections.h: What to do if you break a beaker
p: Do not pick up the glass with your bare hands. Tell the teacher straight away, keep others away from the broken glass, and let the teacher or lab attendant clean it up with a brush and pan.

First term is about our planet: ecosystems, natural resources, environmental hazards, environmental health, waste, climate change and sustainable development. Second term is about living things and matter: cells, tissues, heredity, adaptation, atoms and molecules, changes in matter, water and air, and microorganisms. Third term is about energy, machines, science and technology, ICT and careers.

title: The Ecosystem: Meaning and Components
summary: What an ecosystem is, its living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts, and how producers, consumers and decomposers are grouped.

p: An ecosystem is a community of living things (biotic) interacting with their non-living surroundings (abiotic) in a particular area. It can be as big as an ocean or a desert, or as small as a pond or a rotting log.
The living or once-living parts of an ecosystem are grouped by how they get energy.

Producers (autotrophs) make their own food, usually using sunlight: plants and algae. Consumers (heterotrophs) get energy by eating other living things. Primary consumers eat producers (grasshopper, cow, rabbit; these are herbivores). Secondary consumers eat primary consumers (frog, fox; carnivores or omnivores). Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers (snake, hawk). Decomposers break down dead plants, animals and waste and return nutrients to the soil (bacteria and fungi).
Sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature and salinity (how salty the water is) are the non-living parts. They decide what can live in a place.
Study the table of a typical school garden.

head: Biotic
Abiotic
rows: Water from rain or a tap

p: Everything in an ecosystem depends on something else. Plants need soil, water and sunlight. Animals need plants for food and water to drink. Decomposers need dead organisms to feed on. Plants in turn need the nutrients that decomposers release into the soil.

title: Food Chains, Food Webs and Energy Flow
summary: How energy moves from the sun through producers and consumers, the difference between a food chain and a food web, and the 10% rule.

p: The ultimate source of energy for almost every ecosystem is the Sun. Energy flows in one direction only: from the Sun to producers, then to consumers. It does not go round in a circle (unlike nutrients, which are recycled).

A food chain is a single pathway showing who eats whom. Example: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. The grass is the producer; the grasshopper is the primary consumer; the frog is the secondary consumer; the snake is the tertiary consumer; the hawk is the quaternary (fourth-level) consumer. The arrows show the direction in which energy goes, from the food to the one that eats it. (The lesson note's first list calls the hawk a tertiary consumer; in this chain the snake is tertiary and the hawk is quaternary.)

img.alt: A circular food chain: green plant (producer), grasshopper (primary consumer), frog (secondary consumer), snake (tertiary consumer), hawk and fungi shown as final consumers
img.cap: A food chain. The hawk and the fungi are the last links; fungi break down dead matter.

p: A food web is many food chains joined together. It is more realistic, because most animals eat more than one thing. A hawk, for example, may eat snakes, rats and frogs. If one organism is removed from a web, the others can find other food, so a web is more stable than a single chain.

When a grasshopper eats grass it gets only about 10% of the energy in the grass. The other 90% is lost as heat or used by the plant for living. So at each step up the chain only about 10% of the energy passes on. This is why a food chain is short (usually four or five links), and why the hawk at the top gets very little of the original Sun energy. It is also why there are far fewer hawks than grasshoppers.
Worked example: if the grass holds 10,000 units of energy, the grasshopper gets about 1,000, the frog about 100, the snake about 10 and the hawk about 1.

title: Balance of Nature and the Disruption of Ecosystems
summary: How populations are kept in check, and how deforestation, pollution, overhunting and invasive species upset the balance.

p: In a healthy ecosystem each population is kept in check by food supply, predators and disease. There is a balance between producers, consumers and decomposers. If one part is removed, the whole system is affected. For example, if all the frogs are removed, the grasshoppers may increase hugely and eat all the grass.

sections.h: An example of an invasive species
p: Water hyacinth is a floating plant from South America. It spread over many rivers and lagoons in Nigeria, including around Lagos. It covers the water, blocks sunlight and boats, and takes oxygen from the water, so fish die.
Plant trees, fish and hunt only within limits and seasons set by law, protect forests and wildlife in reserves and national parks, and keep rubbish and chemicals out of rivers.

title: Natural Resources: Renewable and Non-Renewable
summary: What natural resources are, the two types with examples, and where Nigeria's main resources are found.

p: Natural resources are materials from nature that are useful to people. They are 'gifts of nature' used for survival and for the economy. In Nigeria they include crude oil, natural gas, coal, tin, limestone, forests, water, sunlight and fertile soil.

These can be replaced by nature in a fairly short time, so they will not run out if we manage them wisely. Examples: sunlight (solar energy), water (hydropower, replaced by the water cycle), wind, forests (can be replanted) and living things such as crops and animals (which reproduce). Soil is renewable only very slowly, so it must be protected from erosion.

These exist in a fixed amount and took millions of years to form. Once used up, they are gone for a very long time. Examples: fossil fuels (crude oil, natural gas and coal, which come from the remains of ancient plants and animals) and minerals.

title: Importance and Conservation of Natural Resources
summary: How resources support the economy, why depending on one resource is risky, and how to conserve resources with the 3 Rs, afforestation and laws.

p: Government revenue: Nigeria earns most of its government income from selling crude oil, which pays for roads, schools and hospitals. Foreign exchange: selling oil and gas abroad earns foreign money (such as US dollars) used to buy goods we do not make. Raw materials: limestone for cement, timber for furniture and paper, crude oil for petrol, kerosene and plastics. Employment: oil and gas, mining and farming give millions of people jobs.

sections.h: Danger of depending on one resource
p: If a country depends on only one resource, a fall in its price or the running out of the resource can badly damage the economy. That is why Nigeria is encouraged to develop farming, manufacturing, technology and other resources too (diversification).
Conservation is the wise and careful use and protection of resources to prevent waste and running out. We conserve so that the resources will still be there for future generations.

The 3 Rs: Reduce (use less, for example switch off lights), Reuse (use things again, for example refill water bottles), Recycle (turn waste into new products, for example plastic and paper). Afforestation: planting new trees to replace those cut. Using alternatives: moving from petrol and diesel to renewable energy such as solar. Laws: national parks that protect forests and wildlife, and punishments for illegal mining and oil spills.

Walk around the school compound for 15 minutes and list all the natural resources you can see, then say whether each is renewable or not. For example: sunlight (renewable), trees (renewable), water from a tap or well (renewable), wind (renewable), stones and gravel (non-renewable), soil (renewable if protected).

title: Environmental Hazards (1): Drought and Desertification
summary: The meaning, causes, effects and control of drought and desertification, with the Great Green Wall.

p: An environmental hazard is a natural or man-made event that could harm people, property and the environment. When a hazard actually causes harm, it is called a disaster.

A drought is a long period of abnormally low rainfall, leading to a serious shortage of water. Causes: natural changes in the climate, and human activities such as deforestation (trees help to make rain). Effects: crop failure, famine (shortage of food), death of livestock, and rivers and lakes drying up, such as the shrinking of Lake Chad. Control: irrigation (bringing water to farms), afforestation, and dams to store water in the rainy season.

Desertification is the process by which fertile land in dry regions slowly turns into desert. It is a big problem in northern Nigeria (Sokoto, Kano, Borno and other states). Causes: drought; overgrazing (too many cattle and goats eat all the grass and leave the soil bare); and deforestation for firewood, which exposes the soil to sun and wind. Control: planting trees, especially shelter belts that break the wind, and controlled grazing (moving animals from plot to plot so the grass can grow back).

The Great Green Wall is an African-led project to plant a belt of trees and restore land across the Sahel region, south of the Sahara, from Senegal to Djibouti. Nigeria takes part in it. It aims to slow the spread of the desert, bring back farmland and give people jobs.

title: Environmental Hazards (2): Erosion, Flooding and Preparedness
summary: Types and control of soil erosion, causes and prevention of flooding, and how to be prepared for disasters.

p: Soil erosion is the washing or blowing away of the topsoil, the most fertile layer. Wind erosion blows dry, bare soil away (common in the north). Water erosion is when rain washes soil away; it is a massive problem in south-eastern Nigeria, for example the Agulu-Nanka gullies in Anambra State. Causes: deforestation, overgrazing and poor farming such as ploughing down a slope. Control: plant cover crops and trees (roots hold the soil), terracing (cutting steps into a hillside to slow the water) and contour ploughing (ploughing across the slope, not down it).

Flooding is an overflow of water onto land that is normally dry. It is a problem in coastal cities such as Lagos and along rivers such as the Niger and Benue. Causes: heavy rainfall; poor drainage, with gutters and canals blocked by refuse; and building on waterways or drainage channels. Control: build and clear gutters and canals; stop building on waterways (by law); and use dams to control river flow.

Disaster preparedness means taking steps before a hazard strikes to reduce its harm. Examples: listen to warnings from the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) and the flood outlook issued by the government; teach people what to do (for example move to higher ground in a flood); keep emergency food, water and a first-aid kit; and clear gutters before the rainy season starts.
